# @jpisgeek/proton-pass

Proton Pass as a swamp vault provider. `${{ vault.get('<vault>', 'KEY') }}`
resolves live through the official `pass-cli` at run time. This provider copies
no secret into swamp storage, into this repository, or into any file — it writes
no files at all, and caches no value between calls. It cannot make that promise
for the whole host: `pass-cli` keeps its own local database, which is where
Proton Pass data lives on this machine (its key is in the login Keychain on
macOS), and the CLI is an ordinary process with ordinary filesystem access. For
people who keep their lives in the Proton ecosystem and want swamp to read
credentials from the same place everything else does.

**Version** `2026.09.05.1` · **License** MIT · **Source**
https://github.com/jpisgeek/slog-bog/tree/main/proton-pass

## Install

Clone this GitHub repository and register this extension's source in your Swamp
repo. Replace the example path with the canonical location of your clone:

```sh
swamp extension source add /example/slog-bog/proton-pass --only vaults
```

This repaired version is distributed through GitHub source, not a registry
release.

## `@jpisgeek/proton-pass`

Reads secrets from Proton Pass via the official pass-cli. Secrets are never
copied into swamp storage by this provider. Every get() is a live lookup.

### Arguments

| config         | type    | required | default      | description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| -------------- | ------- | -------- | ------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `vaultName`    | string  | yes      |              | Proton Pass vault to read from, e.g. '<your-vault>'                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `defaultField` | string  | no       | `"password"` | Item field used when the secret key names no field                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `timeoutSec`   | integer | no       | `30`         | How long any single pass-cli call may take, in whole seconds, 1 to 300. It reaches Proton's servers, so an unbounded call can hang for as long as the network allows. The range is enforced by the schema and was previously enforced without being stated anywhere. |
| `binary`       | string  | no       | `"pass-cli"` | pass-cli executable. Left as a bare name it is resolved against PATH and then a list of known install locations, because non-login contexts (ssh, launchd, cron, a daemon) often lack Homebrew's bin directory on PATH.                                              |

### Methods

`get(key)` — resolve a secret · `list()` — item names (vault provider contract)

### Data written

_none — a vault writes no resources_

## Example

```yaml
# vaults/proton.yaml
type: "@jpisgeek/proton-pass"
name: proton
config:
  vaultName: <your-vault> # the Proton Pass vault to read from
  defaultField: password # field used when a key names none

# Then in any model:
#   apiKey: ${{ vault.get('proton', 'Example Service/API Key') }}
# Key forms:
#   "Item Title"                 -> that item, field = defaultField
#   "Item Title/fieldname"       -> explicit field on that item
```

## Caveats

Requires the Proton Pass CLI (`brew install proton-pass-cli`) and a usable
session (`pass-cli login`, or a personal access token for unattended runs). On
macOS the CLI's database key lives in the login Keychain, so `get()` works from
a GUI login session or a LaunchAgent in that session, not over plain ssh, from a
LaunchDaemon, or from cron. Add the optional `binary` key under `config` — an
absolute path to `pass-cli` — when the CLI is not on the PATH the swamp process
sees; left unset it is resolved against PATH and then the usual Homebrew
prefixes. THIS PROVIDER IS READ-ONLY. There is no `put()`: create items in the
Proton Pass UI and read them here. Writing was removed deliberately — it
accounted for 10 of 39 review blocks across six rounds, and every one was a way
for a non-idempotent write to be misreported. There is also no
`pass://SHARE_ID/ITEM_ID` addressing; it accounted for 14 more. Items are
addressed by TITLE, so renaming an item in the Proton Pass UI breaks any key
naming it. That is the cost of the smaller surface, and it is the whole of it.

## Security

Every `get()` is a live lookup; no value is cached, logged, or persisted.
pass-cli is invoked with `Deno.Command` (never a shell), so there is no argv
injection. This provider writes nothing at all — not to swamp storage, and not
to Proton. It reads. **Secret keys appear in errors; remote text does not.** A
failed lookup says which key failed — `Secret 'x/y' not found in vault 'z'` —
and that is deliberate. The key and the vault name are what YOU passed in; they
are already in the model definition that asked for the secret, and an error that
will not say which lookup failed makes a secrets provider undiagnosable. Every
such string is length-bounded before it enters an exception, so a pathological
key cannot flood a run log, and control characters in it are escaped rather than
printed: a key containing a newline would otherwise write a second, forged line
into the run log, and an ESC sequence would drive the terminal reading it.
Control characters are refused outright in `vaultName`, `defaultField`, `binary`
and in any secret key — before pass-cli is invoked with them. The pass-cli
executable path is never named in an error either, neither the value you
configured in `binary` nor the install prefix it resolved to: run logs and
reports are the wrong place to publish the filesystem layout of the host swamp
runs on. What is NOT forwarded is anything pass-cli or Proton said. Its stdout
is never placed in an exception at all — for `item view` that stdout is the
whole item, secret included. Its stderr and its `Error:` lines are read only to
classify, and what escapes is one fixed verdict from a closed set:
`session-not-usable`, `vault-not-found`, `item-not-found`, `field-not-found`,
`permission-denied`, `network-failure`, or `unclassified`, which alone carries
the process exit code appended in parentheses — a small integer, the only part
of any verdict that varies, and never text from pass-cli or from Proton. One
further fixed diagnostic escapes outside that set: a macOS login-Keychain
failure (`errSecInteractionNotAllowed`) is reported in its own words, because
"this works from a GUI session but not over ssh" is the whole of the fix and no
verdict name conveys it. It is likewise fixed text, containing nothing pass-cli
or Proton said. No CLI or server text is forwarded verbatim, in any error path.
Exception strings from here reach swamp run logs and reports. **A key splits at
the FIRST `/`.** `Example Service/API Key` means the item `Example Service`,
field `API Key`. An item title containing `/` therefore cannot be addressed at
all, and a key beginning `pass://` is refused outright rather than quietly
treated as a title. Titles containing `/` are also omitted from `list()`:
offering one would hand back a string that resolves to a different item's field,
and `get()` refuses such a key outright when an item genuinely carries that
title. **Vault names and ids are joined to their options.** Both are untrusted —
the vault name is operator input, the ids come off the wire — and either can
begin with `-`. Passed as its own argument, pass-cli's option parser is free to
read one as a flag; using `--option=value` leaves nothing to reinterpret.
Avoiding a shell prevents shell injection, which is a different problem. Ids
taken from the item listing must be canonical base64url before being sent as an
address: the alphabet `A-Z a-z 0-9 _ -`, a length that can actually encode
bytes, `=` only as trailing padding and only in the amount that length requires,
and no bits in the final character that a decoder would discard. Padding is
normalised before any id is compared, because `TQ` and `TQ==` are one value to a
decoder and comparing spellings would check one id while pass-cli executed
another. Every id a real vault returns is 86 base64url characters plus `==`.
Earlier versions of this provider documented base64url while accepting
impossible lengths and padding; the code now means what this paragraph says. The
address sent to pass-cli and the address checked for liveness have to be the
same string, and `%2F` is one character to a CLI that decodes it and five to a
check that does not. Vault scope itself is enforced by pass-cli: `--vault-name=`
is passed on every call. The binding below is a different, weaker thing and is
worth stating precisely — the expected ids come from the item LISTING, so
comparing them against the item view proves that two responses agree, not that
either describes an item in your configured vault. It catches a confused CLI,
not a hostile one. A lookup is bound to the id, the share, the vault and the
title it resolved to, and the response must agree with all three. The title
matters because resolution reads the listing and then views the item by id:
rename the item between those two calls and the id still resolves, so without
the check the secret would come back under a title that no longer names it.
**Deleted means deleted, WHEN `state` is present.** Proton Pass moves an item to
the trash rather than purging it. This provider reads `state` from both the
listing and the item body: a row it reports as `Trashed` is not listed and not
resolvable, so deleting a secret stops it being handed out. Previously it did
not — the item stayed visible as an available key and `--item-title` would
resolve to it. The qualifier is real and is the operator-decision below: a row
with NO `state` field is treated as live, because older pass-cli builds omit it
and hiding every secret from them would be worse. Against such a build, deletion
is not a reliable revocation signal. **A title must identify exactly one live
item, addressed by id.** Real vaults accumulate items sharing a title, and
`pass-cli --item-title` silently picks one of them. A lookup that matches more
than one active item is refused by name; a lookup that matches one is
re-addressed by that item's id. `--item-title` is never sent. If the item list
gives no id for the matching row, the lookup FAILS rather than falling back to
title selection. When a title matches more than one live item, remove the
duplicates: with URI addressing gone there is no way to name one of several
same-titled items, and guessing is exactly what this refusal exists to prevent.
Titles are compared TWICE, and deliberately not the same way both times.
Ambiguity is judged on a folded form — NFC-normalised, variation selectors in
both the BMP and supplementary ranges removed, trimmed — so that two items which
RENDER identically collide and refuse instead of each matching one request and
returning a confidently wrong secret. Selection is then exact: the single
surviving item must carry byte-for-byte the title you asked for. A title that
merely renders the same as the stored one is refused with a message saying so,
because folding is there to catch collisions, not to guess which item you meant.
Copy titles from `list()`. **Responses are read at named locations only.** The
value returned by `get()` comes from exactly three places in
`item view --output json`, and nowhere else: a value slot inside the typed block
at `content.content` — a tagged union keyed by item type, `{"Login":{…}}`,
`{"Note":{…}}` and so on, from which only `password`, `username`, `email`,
`totp_uri` and `note` are readable by name — the item's own `content.note`,
which is where a note lives when the key asks for one — or a custom field in
`content.extra_fields`, looked up by its name. The earlier wording said two and
named the third in passing. The item is NOT searched for a key matching whatever
field you asked for, which is how an arbitrary string in a response (a share id,
an error message) could previously be retrieved as a secret just by naming it. A
block naming two item types at once is refused rather than chosen between, and a
slot holding an empty string counts as absent: pass-cli writes `""` for a field
that was never filled in, and returning that would hand back an empty credential
and call it success. Inside a field's `content`, only the `Hidden`, `Text` and
`Totp` wrappers hold a value; an unrecognised wrapper is refused rather than
skimmed for the first string in it, which used to return the field's LABEL as
the secret. The item body is parsed against an explicit key list with no
catchall, so a response this provider cannot fully account for — an error
envelope, a diagnostics blob, an unrecognised key — is refused rather than read.
So is an ambiguous one: two documented locations offering different values for
the same field, a field named twice, or two populated content wrappers all fail
the lookup instead of resolving by precedence. This is fail-closed by design; a
pass-cli that grows a new response key will need this provider updated rather
than quietly handing back a guess. Item listings are held to the same rule and
not a weaker one: NO key beyond the set a real `item list` emits — `id`,
`share_id`, `vault_id`, `state`, `flags`, `create_time`, `modify_time`, `title`
and `item_type`, plus `name` as a tolerated alias for `title` — and the wrapped
form carries `items` and nothing else. Of those, `id`, `share_id`, `vault_id`,
`title`, `item_type` and `state` are READ and compared; the rest are recognised
so a real response parses and are never used as a value. Every one of them is
OPTIONAL, and that is a real limit rather than an oversight. A row that omits
`share_id` is accepted, and the share binding then has nothing to compare
against — identity is verified WHEN PRESENT, because older pass-cli builds emit
less than 2.3.2 does and refusing them outright would hide every secret rather
than the wrong one. What is never accepted is a key nobody recognises, a value
of the wrong type, or a `state` that is present and is not exactly `Active` or
`Trashed`. A response can therefore be thin, but it cannot be surprising. An
unrecognised state is REFUSED rather than filed under trashed — quietly dropping
such a row shortens the inventory, and a short inventory is how the
duplicate-title refusal below stops seeing the duplicate and hands back one of
several items without saying which. Every non-blank row must parse, an
unrecognised shape is an error, and empty output is an error rather than "this
vault has no secrets". **Where the strictness stops, precisely.** The OUTER
shapes are closed: the response envelope, the item body, `content`, each listing
row and each custom field entry list their keys exactly and refuse any other.
Two places are deliberately OPEN records, and saying "unknown keys are refused"
without naming them would overstate the guarantee. `content.content` is a union
keyed by item type — `Login`, `Note`, `CreditCard` and whatever Proton adds next
— so enumerating it would refuse a whole item type the day one appears; it is
held to naming exactly ONE type instead, and that type must agree with the row's
`item_type`. A custom field's `content` wrapper is open for the same reason, and
only the documented `Hidden`, `Text` and `Totp` wrappers are ever read from it.
In both cases the keys are unconstrained; what is read from them is not. Two
arrays are accepted with their ELEMENTS unexamined, for the same reason and with
the same limit: `flags` on a listing row or an item body, and `attachments` on
the response envelope. Both must be arrays — a string or an object where an
array belongs is refused — but what is inside them is not inspected, because
nothing here reads either one. They are recognised so a real response parses. If
a future pass-cli puts something meaningful in them, this provider passes it
over rather than refusing it, which is the one place the fail-closed rule bends
to keep real responses working. A response must also be ABOUT the item that was
requested. `item view` is invoked by id, and when the body carries an id it must
be that id; when it carries a state it must not be a trashed one. A field that
is PRESENT but of the wrong type — a numeric id, an object state — is refused
rather than treated as absent: absence is tolerated because older builds
genuinely omit these fields, and letting a wrong-typed value read as absent
would make the one shape a confused response actually takes the one shape that
skips the check. Liveness read from the listing and liveness claimed by the
response are two separate claims, and a cache or a race can make them disagree.
Responses are decoded with strict UTF-8 — invalid bytes are refused rather than
silently rewritten to U+FFFD, which could repair a malformed response into
well-formed JSON and alter a title, an id, or the secret itself on the way in.
And an object that names the same key twice is refused: `JSON.parse` keeps the
last and discards the first before any check can run, so
`{"state":"Trashed","state":"Active"}` would otherwise reach the liveness test
as unambiguously live. **pass-cli gets a named environment and a named path.**
The CLI is spawned with a cleared environment and only these variables: `PATH`,
`HOME`, `USER`, `LOGNAME`, `TMPDIR`, `LANG`, `LC_ALL`, `LC_CTYPE`,
`XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, `XDG_DATA_HOME`, `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`,
`DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS` — enough for PATH lookup, the macOS login Keychain,
and a Linux secret store. It does not inherit swamp's environment, which is
shared with every other extension in the run and can hold unrelated API tokens
and proxy or TLS overrides. `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` is deliberately excluded. The VALUES
are checked too, not just the names: the directory-valued variables must be
absolute paths and `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS` must name `unix:` sockets and
nothing else — a D-Bus address is a semicolon-separated LIST and a client may
use any element of it, so every element is checked, not just the first. That
variable selects a transport and accepts `tcp:host=…`, which would point the
secret store somewhere else entirely with no TLS involved. `PATH` is filtered to
its absolute entries before the child sees it, so a `.` or empty component
cannot select a helper from the working directory. A value failing its rule is
dropped rather than corrected, so the child sees the variable unset — a state it
already has to handle. If pass-cli needs a variable not on this list on your
host, it will not see it. `binary` must be either the bare name `pass-cli` or an
ABSOLUTE path: a relative path like `./pass-cli` is refused, because it would
resolve against whatever directory the swamp process happens to be in. **What
this provider does not promise.** An item whose `state` field is absent is
treated as live, because older pass-cli builds omit it and hiding every secret
from them would be worse than the bug that reading `state` fixes. The pass-cli
executable itself is trusted on identity: whichever binary answers `--version`
first — the first `pass-cli` on an absolute PATH entry, one of the Homebrew
prefixes, or whatever absolute path `binary` names, which is taken on trust
without a probe — receives your item titles, vault name, and nothing verifies
its ownership, signature or digest. Titles that differ only by CONFUSABLE
characters across scripts — a Cyrillic `А` in `EXAMPLE-А-KEY` against a Latin
`A` — are not detected as duplicates: catching those needs Unicode's confusables
table, which is large, versioned, and not something this provider vendors.
Composition, trailing whitespace and variation selectors ARE caught;
cross-script lookalikes are not. Pinning a digest would break on every CLI
release, so the lever is yours: set `binary` to an absolute path in a directory
you control if PATH is not trustworthy on that host. And every call is a live
lookup with a bounded timeout: nothing is cached, so a Proton outage is a
failure rather than a stale success. `timeoutSec` bounds the WHOLE call,
locating the executable included, and a wedged candidate used to burn its own
five-second probe timeout after the deadline you set had already passed. **How
the executable is chosen, exactly.** An ABSOLUTE `binary` path is used as given
and is NOT probed — you named a specific file, and this provider runs that file.
A bare name must be `pass-cli`; anything else is refused rather than resolved.
Resolving the bare name walks the absolute entries of `PATH` in order, probing
each with `--version`, and then the standard install prefixes. The candidate
count therefore depends on the length of your `PATH` and is not fixed. Relative
`PATH` entries are skipped: what resolution returns is always an absolute path,
so that the file which answered the probe is the file that later receives your
item titles.

See [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/jpisgeek/slog-bog/blob/main/SECURITY.md)
for the repository's security review requirements. This version is shared as
GitHub source and is not published to the Swamp registry.
